title: How we run our agents on a model 14× cheaper than Opus
summary: Most of our agents now run on GLM 5.3 Flash, which costs $18 per 1,000 tasks... whereas Opus 5.5 costs $254. I'm publishing every eval score behind that choice (including where GLM fails).
body_markdown:
*The premium model wins the demo, and it should. The argument starts when the bill arrives.*


You open Claude Code, hand it a messy, long-running task, go get a coffee and come back to working code. Then you try the same job on a cheaper model and spend the afternoon fixing small mistakes. If you have lived this, the conclusion feels obvious: premium models win, and building agents on anything else is saving pennies to lose hours.


We won't argue with the experience; it matches ours. We run our agents on GLM 5.3 Flash anyway, a model 14× cheaper than Opus 5.5, and every eval score is public, including the checks the cheap model fails. The mental math skips two things: what "better" costs, and how much of the gap is the model at all.


While we were updating this post in early November 2026, a tweet reporting that[Revolut is moving to self-hosted GLM](https://twitter.com/guilleflorvs/status/2117379073785696395) sat on the Hacker News front page. The math below is our version of that trade: premium models everywhere versus the right model for each task.


## Where the expensive models genuinely win


Let's concede the whole list first. On complex, long-running tasks, a frontier model like Opus 5.5 makes fewer wrong turns when your instructions are ambiguous. It self-corrects better over a long horizon. It needs less hand-holding: fewer retries and dead ends, fewer of those moments where the agent confidently walks into a wall. If the task is genuinely hard, the difference is real and you can feel it.


A comparison that hid this gap would be marketing, so we show ours with the gap visible.


## Our evals, gaps included


We ran 15 tasks taken from real work on our platform (we build Vybe, so weigh our numbers accordingly), across sales, marketing and recruiting, from easy to hard. Each task has a checklist: the facts a good answer must include, the instructions it must follow, the mistakes it must avoid, like inventing a detail or editing a file it was only asked to read. Deterministic checks and a separate AI judge review every run from a fresh agent, and cost is not part of the score. All of it is public on our[model showcase](https://www.vybe.build/models/showcase) , scores averaged over five runs per task. The numbers below are the current showcase figures, re-checked against the page on November 3, 2026.


Average score by team:


Team GLM 5.3 Flash Opus 5.5 GPT-6 Astra


Sales 96.2% 97.4% 99.5%


Marketing 97.1% 99.0% 98.4%


Recruiting 95.0% 99.7% 100%


Recruiting shows the widest gap: 95.0% for GLM against 99.7% for Opus and a full 100% for GPT-6 Astra. Those are real gaps. A 95 is not a 99 when a missed check means a wrong answer reaches a candidate.


Cost per 1,000 tasks at public provider rates:


Team GLM 5.3 Flash Opus 5.5 You save


Sales $15 $251 94%


Marketing $18 $254 93%


Recruiting $19 $251 92%


GPT-6 Astra sits at $662 per 1,000 tasks, 2.6× the Opus price.


One concrete example from the showcase: the three models got a marketing task, analyze a 90-day Search Console export and propose fixes.


Model Effort Cost per run Time Score


GLM 5.3 Flash Max $0.012 2.2 min 98.2%


Opus 5.5 Medium $0.23 56s 100%


GPT-6 Astra Medium $0.50 70s 100%


The cheap model missed fewer than two checks in a hundred. The premium models paid 19× to 42× more than GLM to close that last stretch. Whether that stretch matters depends on the task.


## What the gap costs at scale


Those per-task prices look tiny. At 10,000 tasks a month, the all-Opus bill is $2,540 and the GLM bill is $180. The difference is $2,360 every month, about $28,000 a year. We wrote before about[how we cut our AI agent bill](https://www.vybe.build/blog/how-to-cut-your-ai-agent-bill) . This is the same logic applied to model choice.


"Better" is only a useful word once it has a price. An extra 2.6 points of average checklist completion (96.1% for GLM against 98.7% for Opus across the three teams) is rarely worth $28,000 a year. If your workload is twenty genuinely hard tasks a month and ten thousand easy ones, run the twenty on the premium model. Your premium bill for the month comes to about five dollars.


## Model choice is set per task


The trade exists because model choice is set per task: per agent, per scheduled task, per skill and even per step inside an agent. The same agent can draft customer replies on a frontier model while a scheduled task tags support tickets on the cheap one. If you are evaluating agent platforms, ask where the model choice lives. When one model has to do everything, you end up with the all-premium bill or the all-cheap quality loss. A mixed setup avoids both.


One of our engineers, Yann, describes the goal like this: "our job is to get Vybe as close as possible to that experience through various AI engineering efforts". Routing, retry logic, prompts, guardrails: a good part of the "Claude Code feels better" experience is engineering around the model. Engineering iterates faster than weights do, so we work on closing the gap instead of paying for it on every task.


## The onboarding question we have not answered


Yann has also been asking something we don't have a clean answer to. In his words: "I wonder how different the user experience would be if we are using more premium models for the onboarding?"


His point deserves better than a shrug. First impressions form in the first session, and onboarding is short, ambiguous and guidance-heavy, the kind of interaction where premium models are at their best. The cost math allows a hybrid policy: route the first session through a premium model, then hand the steady-state work to GLM 5.3 Flash. At the showcase's $0.25 per Opus task, a new user's first ten tasks cost about $2.50 even at premium rates, because onboarding is a small share of the calls a user will ever make.


The risks are real. Two models behave differently, and a user who gets a brilliant first session and a slightly sloppier second one may read that as the product degrading. Mixing models also means two sets of failure modes to debug. We have not shipped any of this. Read the whole section as a working hypothesis.


## What would settle it


Everything above is argument and arithmetic. Proof would look like this: task completion rate and retries per task, onboarding drop-off, time to first successful outcome and cost per completed task, each measured for a premium-onboarding group against a cheap-everywhere group. We have not run that experiment. When we do, we will publish it either way.


In the end, "better" only means something once you attach a workload: a task, a price and a failure mode you can live with. We run a model 14× cheaper than Opus and we publish the evals showing where it loses. The premium experience is a fine product too. The interesting question, the one Yann keeps asking, is how much of the distance between the two turns out to be engineering.
